item.title: The Human Brain Owes Its Existence to a Prehistoric Pandemic
item.description:
Genetics

The Human Brain Owes Its Existence to a Prehistoric Pandemic

How an ancient viral infection helped form humankind.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • A retroviral infection is responsible for evolution of the human brain from chimpanzee ancestors.
  • The viral DNA regulates genes that drive brain development.
  • The viral DNA is not a gene, so it eluded researchers looking for genes responsible for human brain evolution.
Source: R. Douglas Fields

Seven million years ago, the evolution of humans and chimpanzees suddenly split from their common ancestor. New research finds that a retroviral infection inserted viral DNA into the genome of early chimpanzees can account for the enormous increase in size and cognitive power of the human brain.

Remarkably, humans and chimpanzees share 98.8 percent of the same genes, but the differences between chimps and humans are astonishing. The human brain is three times bigger than the chimp brain, our closest evolutionary ancestor. That enormous brain gives humans unparalleled superintelligence for complex thought, language, and technology, from stone tools to supercomputers to spacecraft. But, the transformation of the human brain is not easily accounted for by the few genes that differ between us and chimps. How the human brain suddenly ballooned in size and achieved unsurpassed cognitive power is a long-standing mystery in evolutionary biology.

A new study published this week in the journal Science Advances has uncovered a surprising answer. A retroviral infection seven million years ago split the evolution of the human brain from that of chimpanzees.

The difference between humans and chimps is not so much in their genes, but rather in how human genes are controlled. There are many complex mechanisms regulating when a particular gene is turned on or off, which operate through stretches of DNA between genes, called introns. Chemical modifications of DNA, called epigenetic regulation, also dictate whether or not specific genes are expressed. The new study finds that an ancient viral infection affected how key genes for brain development are controlled.

Viral Hacking Into DNA

Retroviruses, like the HIV virus, do not have the cellular machinery to replicate themselves. Instead, they hijack a cell’s genetic program to force it to make viral proteins. The retroviruses reverse engineer the normal process of DNA making RNA to make proteins, by slipping their viral RNA into cells. This gets converted into DNA, and when the cell reads out its genetic program, it unwittingly makes viral RNA and viral proteins, much like malicious code hacked into a computer program.

Snippets of DNA from retroviruses can get integrated into germline cells and passed on for generations. Typically, these fragments of viral DNA no longer make viral proteins, but they alter how genes are regulated. Eight percent of the human and chimpanzee genome consists of snippets of DNA hacked into their genome by ancient retroviral infections, according to the authors. Sometimes retroviral DNA causes dreadful diseases, but other times, the changes in the way genes are expressed can produce beneficial effects that can cause a sudden evolutionary change or even launch a new species.

article continues after advertisement

Retroviral DNA Regulates Genes that Control Brain Development

The new study, led by Johan Jakobsson of Lund University in Sweden, identified a snippet of retroviral DNA, called PTERV1, inserted into chimpanzee DNA. This retroviral DNA, which is absent in humans, does not make a protein, but it alters how other genes are expressed. PTERV1 is heavily modified by methylation, an epigenetic means of silencing genes. The researchers found that this retroviral DNA silenced a human-specific RNA (LILNC00662) that controls many other genes important for brain development.

The researchers used chimpanzee and human stem cells to create organoids (‘minibrains’) in cell culture. This enabled them to insert PTERV1 into the human organoids and remove it from the chimpanzee organoids. LILNC00662 was completely absent in the chimpanzee minibrains, because the PTERV1 insert blocked its genetic readout by causing an epigenetic change (methylation) that suppresses gene expression.

Human minibrains, which lack PTERV1, expressed LILNC00662 at high levels, and they also expressed many other genes important for neural development that LILNC00662 activates. Using various means to manipulate the expression of LILC00622, the researchers found that when this RNA was silenced in human minibrains, neural development was impaired. When they deleted PTERV1 in chimpanzee minibrains, LILNC00662 was expressed as it is in human brains.

Since PTERV1 is completely absent from humans, the authors theorize that it must have resulted from a retroviral infection in the ancestors of African apes about 5 to 7 million years ago. They surmise that either the human and chimpanzee ancestors did not occupy the same habitat at the time of the viral infection, or the human ancestors were resistant to this infection. Evidence in favor of the latter hypothesis is that humans have a protein (TRIM5alpha) with antiviral activity that could have prevented humans from being infected.

Viral DNA Hidden Between Genes

Those seeking to identify what genes in humans could account for our superior brain would not detect this DNA insert because it does not code for a gene itself. It acts by regulating the readout of many other genes that are shared by chimpanzees and humans to guide brain development.

This is an interesting example of evolution that does not conform to classical Darwinian mechanisms of selecting favorable traits from minor variations over generations. In this case, a sudden major morphological and physiological change in a species occurs, because the engine of evolution, DNA, is suddenly hijacked by a virus.

article continues after advertisement

Pandemics are scourges, but one that afflicted primates millions of years ago separated the evolution of chimpanzees from humans and gave rise to the extraordinary human brain. Ironically, the most advanced brain on earth owes its existence to the most primitive form of life there is.

item.title: Vote to Live: Staying Empowered Amid Unanswered Questions
item.description:
Depression

Vote to Live: Staying Empowered Amid Unanswered Questions

Voting gives you a voice despite uncertainties. Here's how to make yours heard.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Some questions, like Nolan Wells' cause of death, may stay open, but local elections still shape the answers.
  • Psychologists say taking part in your community can lift mood and ease feelings of hopelessness.

I’m still mad about Nolan Wells. I’m still sad. I still have questions, and some nights I wake up with worry on my heart for my own sweet innocent Black baby boy. Nolan was 18. He was a wide receiver from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, with a whole life ahead of him. I’ve talked to my family and friends, and I keep thinking about Nolan’s family, who are still waiting for answers, and about our babies whose futures we’re supposed to protect.

If you’ve felt that heaviness too, you’re not alone. Some days, I feel helpless. Some days, the hopelessness creeps in and won’t leave. I’m writing this because I know a lot of us are carrying the same thing, and because I know it’s the perfect time for us to do something with it.

What We Know About Nolan’s Case

Nolan Xavier Wells disappeared after a July 4 boat trip to Horn Island. His body was found days later. The Jackson County Sheriff’s Office did not investigate his death as a homicide.

In September, a Jackson County grand jury returned a “no true bill,” meaning no one was indicted. More than three months later, the cause of his death is still unknown. The state autopsy and the independent autopsy his family commissioned both listed the cause and manner of death as undetermined. The district attorney says the case is closed. The family, through attorney Ben Crump, says it isn’t, and they’re asking for a federal investigation.

I won’t tell you what happened to Nolan. Nobody can say that yet, but his family deserves the truth. And his case shows why the answers we get depend on the people in power we choose to serve and protect us.

Some Answers Won’t Come Before Election Day

The honest truth is that some questions won’t be answered by November. Investigations take time. Autopsies, grand juries, and lawsuits move on their own schedules. Sometimes the answers never arrive at all.

That uncertainty is painful. But it doesn’t mean we’re powerless.

Power Doesn’t Require Certainty

We don’t need every answer to take meaningful action. Researchers have found that people who feel some sense of control over their lives tend to handle stress better, even when circumstances are out of their hands. Control doesn’t mean knowing everything. It means choosing what you do next.

That’s where behavioral activation comes in. Therapists use this approach when people feel stuck: you take a small, values-based step first, and the sense of agency follows. Voting works this way. You don’t have to feel sure about everything to do it. You just have to decide that your voice belongs in the room.

article continues after advertisement

Choose Who Answers the Questions

A lot of the answers we’re waiting for come from people we elect. The ballot decides who holds the roles that shape what gets investigated, what gets reported, and how families get treated.

District attorneys decide what cases go before a grand jury and what evidence gets presented. Sheriffs run the offices that investigate deaths. Coroners and medical examiners determine causes of death, though how those roles get filled varies by state and county. School board members decide how discipline gets handled in your child’s school. Judges and city councils shape the rules that govern daily life. Some decisions happen at the federal level, but many of the most immediate ones happen close to home.

So when you fill out your ballot, go beyond the top race. Look up who holds these roles where you live, and ask whether you trust them to answer hard questions openly.

Ask Better Questions

Voting is one way to act. Asking good questions is another, and it doesn’t require picking a side. You can research candidates, officeholders, or local leaders:

  • How do they handle investigations involving deaths or serious harm to young people?
  • Are reports and findings made public? If not, why not?
  • How will a candidate’s office communicate with families who are still waiting for answers?
  • What will a candidate do to make sure people are treated fairly when they have questions?

Write down what you learn. Compare answers. Then vote with what you value.

Staying Steady While You Wait

When the worry gets loud, a plan can steady you:

  • Pick one action you control. Check your registration. Request a mail ballot. Ask one question at your next local meeting.
  • Contact a local official or office with questions. Write down your questions. Demand answers. Hold elected officials accountable to being transparent and giving information to the public.
  • Limit the news loop. Check updates on a schedule, not every hour. Mute distressing hashtags and don’t engage with triggering content. Constant refreshing can feed hopelessness.
  • Fine community. Connect with a friend, a loved one, or a neighbor. Waiting is easier when you’re not doing it alone.
article continues after advertisement

And if the sleepless nights and the hopelessness keep showing up, that’s worth talking through with a licensed therapist. You don’t have to carry the burden by yourself.

Healing Is Collective

Shawn Ginwright’s work on radical healing reminds us that we don’t get through uncertainty alone. Healing happens in community, when people recover their voice and power together. At Nolan’s funeral in Ocean Springs, Ben Crump led the mourners in a chant that his life matters. That collective cry allows for collective healing in real time. Ignacio Martín-Baró’s liberation psychology pushes us further: instead of only helping people cope with harmful conditions, those of us who have the capacity also have the responsibility to work to change those conditions.

Source: Isha W Metzger

Keep Asking After Election Day

That means showing up after the election, too. Attend school board and county meetings. Support families who are still waiting. Keep records of what you’re told and follow up when promises slip. Staying engaged between elections is part of what makes voting matter.

Get Ready in Five Steps

Early voting is currently underway, and Election Day is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Here’s how to be ready, wherever you live:

  • Check your registration. Start at vote.gov, which links to every state’s official site. If you’re not registered, find out whether your state’s deadline has passed.
  • Know your options. Find out whether your state offers early voting, mail ballots, or both, and what the deadline is to request a mail ballot.
  • Find your polling place. Election Day locations can differ from early voting sites. Confirm yours before you go.
  • Know the ID rules. Requirements vary, and many states require photo ID. If you need one, your election office can tell you about free options.
  • Make the plan. Pick a day, a time, and a route. Put it in your phone with a reminder, and text the people you’re going with.
article continues after advertisement

Nolan was 18. He would have been old enough to vote for the first time this November. You can’t control every answer. You can control whether your voice shows up in the rooms where answers get made. Pick your date. Make your plan. Let’s stay in the question together, and let’s make sure we’re part of the answer.

item.title: If There's One Thing You Need From a Friend, This Is It
item.description:
Friends

If There's One Thing You Need From a Friend, This Is It

Feeling safe enough to be yourself is the key to healthy friendships.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Our friendship needs change less than our lives do.
  • Women want friends who listen without judgment.
  • Understanding and acceptance outweigh advice and solutions.

As someone who’s spent much of my career studying friendship, I thought I had a fairly good idea what women needed from friendships. Still, I was curious to see what would emerge when women across the lifespan were asked this question. I reviewed hundreds of responses from women in their 20s through their 70s about what they needed most from the women and friends in their lives. Their answers offered a glimpse into what women value most in their friendships. This follows up an earlier post on what women need from their partners.

Across the responses, I kept seeing variations on the same theme. Whether women talked about support, trust, understanding, acceptance, loyalty, or being truly heard, they seemed to be describing different facets of the same need: emotionally safe friendships. I expected the answers to vary considerably by age. After all, women's lives often look quite different at 25, 45, and 75. Instead, what struck me was how similar the responses were. Across the lifespan, what we need from our friends may not change nearly as much as we think, even if the way we express those needs does.

These insights came from my online survey that grew out of a 2018 Psychology Today post exploring what women want from men in romantic relationships. Between 2018 and 2023, 108 women completed the survey, sharing their perspectives on the qualities they value most in a partner. Although the respondents do not represent a scientific sample of all women, their responses offer a revealing glimpse into the characteristics many associate with healthy, satisfying relationships.

We Never Outgrow the Need for Support

Support was the most frequently mentioned need across age groups, and some women answered with just that one word: support. Others expanded on what support meant to them, describing a need for "unconditional support" and friendships that would "build each other up instead of tearing each other down." Across the lifespan, women repeatedly expressed a desire for friends who would be dependable, encouraging, and present during challenging times.

What struck me was that support wasn't described as rescuing, fixing, or solving problems. Instead, women described wanting friends who would stay present during life's inevitable challenges. Support, in other words, isn't about taking away someone's struggle. It's about making sure she doesn't have to carry it alone.

Women Want to Be Understood, Not Just Heard

Being understood was another recurring need. One respondent wrote that she needed "understanding without judgment." Another said she longed for women who could understand that one’s experiences don’t need to match another’s in order to show empathy. This distinction is important. Listening is about slowing down enough to hear someone's words. Understanding goes deeper. It requires us to put aside our own assumptions long enough to appreciate another person's experiences.

article continues after advertisement

As I read these responses, I was reminded of how often people rush to offer advice when what is actually needed is validation. Many women seemed to be saying, "I don't need you to solve this. I need you to understand what it's like to live it." It’s a different request. I’ve had more than one client share that they don’t take their problems to partners because partners want to find solutions, not simply let them share their stories. Fixes are helpful in their own time, but sometimes people need room to tell their stories before they’re ready to hear solutions.

Acceptance Matters More Than Agreement

One of the strongest themes across all age groups was the desire for less judgment. Women repeatedly mentioned wanting "support without judgment," "acceptance," and "the ability and safety to talk about life experiences without criticism or judgment." One older participant wrote that she wanted "someone to talk to that isn't judgmental and full of advice . . . someone who knows how to listen."

As a counselor, that response lingered with me. In a culture fueled by comparison and endless self-improvement messages, many women seemed to be describing a longing for relationships where they don't have to perform, compete, or prove themselves. They simply want to be accepted for who they are.

Friendship Is Not About Competition

Younger women, in particular, frequently referenced competition among women. Some explicitly wished women would "stop seeing other women as competitors." Others talked about wanting more compassion, kindness, and mutual support. Although concerns about comparison appeared most frequently among younger women, versions of this theme emerged across age groups.

article continues after advertisement

Friendship thrives when there is enough emotional space for everyone to succeed. It is difficult to feel close to someone if you suspect she is quietly keeping score. Perhaps one of the greatest gifts women can offer one another is freedom from comparison. We know that misery loves company, but being there to celebrate a friend’s successes is every bit as important.

As We Age, Friendship May Become Even More Precious

The biggest surprise came from the oldest women. Their answers weren't fundamentally different from younger women's answers. They still wanted support, understanding, trust, and acceptance. What seemed different was the way they described those needs. Older respondents were more likely to talk about companionship, connection, and simply having someone to talk with. One woman said she wanted "a good listener." Another wrote that she needed "friendship and camaraderie." A third described needing "someone who understands and is there."

As we grow older, friendship circles often become smaller and more selective. Our friends may move away, relationships can change, and losses accumulate. These realities may help explain why companionship, connection, and simply having someone who is "there" felt especially meaningful in the responses of older women.

A Friendship Check-In

As you think about your own friendships, consider these questions:

  • Do my friends feel heard when they talk to me?
  • Am I more likely to offer advice or understanding?
  • Do the women in my life know they can be vulnerable without being judged?
  • Am I building other women up, or unintentionally comparing myself to them?
  • Who in my life might benefit from a phone call, a text, or a reminder that they're not alone?
article continues after advertisement

The women in this survey differed in age, life circumstances, and life experiences, yet their answers pointed in the same direction. Beneath our hopes for friendship lies a common desire. We want to know there is someone who will listen, understand, and stay. If there's one thing women seem to need most from their friends, it’s the experience of feeling safe enough to be fully themselves.

item.title: When Your 50/50 Cofounder Partnership Hides a Power Struggle
item.description:
Persuasion

When Your 50/50 Cofounder Partnership Hides a Power Struggle

Equal equity rarely means equal influence, and silence about it slows decisions.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • An even equity split is often a way to avoid an uncomfortable conversation about power.
  • Role, expertise and charisma give cofounders unequal influence even with identical equity.
  • When authority goes unnamed, decisions default to slow consensus.
  • Agree in writing who owns which decisions and how a cofounder-level tie will be broken.
Source: Dall-E/OpenAI

At the start, the even split felt like the most generous thing you could offer. Neither of you would sit above the other. Then decisions slowed. A hire stalled because you couldn’t agree on the candidate. A hard call went unmade. Lately, one of you has started deciding things alone, and the other has gone quiet in meetings.

If you are the one deciding, it can feel like sitting in the passenger seat while the car drifts toward a wall, and you reach for the wheel. If you are the one going quiet, you’ve stopped pushing back because the outcome seems settled before you open your mouth.

Two cofounders I worked with had a version of this dynamic. Before founding their company, one had managed the other. The CTO left the company they had both worked for largely because he expected, as a cofounder, to be included in nearly every significant decision, including those outside his own functional domain. The CEO wanted the opposite: fewer decisions by consensus, more authority to act, and more speed.

When their roles blurred, the CTO felt slighted each time he was not consulted, and the CEO came to regard his partner’s requests for input as insecurity and a grab for status—sacrificing speed for power. On their leadership team, the conflict produced repeated deadlocks and a pattern of executives lining up behind one founder or the other. Before any single decision could move forward, the two of them had to do substantial alignment work.

Equal Ownership, Unequal Influence

Many founding teams arrive at an equal split because the conversation about power feels too threatening to have, particularly when the cofounders are close friends or spouses.

Declaring the partnership 50/50 functions as a gesture of goodwill, and it spares both people a negotiation that might expose disagreement early.

In a study of how founding teams divide ownership, the economists Thomas Hellmann and Noam Wasserman (2011) found that roughly a third of teams in their sample split equity equally, that those teams frequently reached the decision within a day, and that equal splits were associated with lower valuations in the first round of outside financing. In my clinical reading, a decision of that magnitude made that quickly often reflects a conversation the founders avoided. Equal partnerships can work well; the difficulty comes from unexamined, superficial alignment that breaks under stress.

article continues after advertisement

Ownership also says little about influence. In their classic analysis of social power, the social psychologists John French and Bertram Raven (1959) distinguished several sources of influence. Three are especially visible in founding teams.

  • Legitimate power derives from a recognized role, which is why a CEO title carries weight that a CTO title usually does not.

  • Expert power derives from knowledge others depend on, such as ownership of the codebase or the investor relationships.

  • Referent power derives from being admired and identified with, the founder whom employees naturally gravitate toward.

Two people can hold identical equity and very different amounts of each, and employees typically perceive the difference before either founder names it. Prior relationships carry their own hierarchy into the new company as well, which is what happened to the two former colleagues.

What Unspoken Power Does to the Partnership

When authority is undefined, decisions tend to default to consensus, and consensus is slow.

Information begins to collect around whichever founder is moving faster, the other founder loses context, and the executive team reorganizes itself around that asymmetry. Over time, influence that cannot be discussed openly moves underground into side conversations, unilateral calls and withheld information. The founder with less power often withdraws, which is an understandable response to repeatedly feeling unheard.

Beneath most of these struggles, I see one of two movements.

Some founders reach for control. If this is you, the reach usually begins with feeling unrecognized or powerless, or with resentment that your contribution outweighs your share. Once you have lost confidence in your cofounder’s judgment, taking the wheel feels like protecting the company. The cost is that your cofounder feels more insecure, more powerless, and less recognized, and that impact is yours to own.

Other founders let go of control. This can come from a habit of placating, from anxiety about being solely accountable for outcomes, or from the private knowledge that the role has outgrown you. Many of the cofounders I see in this position care deeply about the company and are not keeping pace with its growth. You may try to keep the gap from being seen. Deliverables slip, your cofounder steps in, and you are left failing your own expectations and someone else’s at once, which is among the more painful experiences in a founding team.

article continues after advertisement

Bringing Power Into the Open

Naming the dynamic out loud is uncomfortable, and leaving it unnamed is worse.

Clinicians in training are taught that asking a patient directly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea; a review of the research by Dazzi and colleagues (2014) found no evidence that asking increases suicidal ideation.

Power between cofounders works similarly. Once a power dynamic has been named, the two founders can negotiate it, check in on it, and make explicit agreements about it.

So before you sit down together, ask yourself which way you lean. When a decision stalls, do you take over, or do you defer and go quiet? What did you each expect cofounder status to mean when you started, and did either of you ever say it aloud?

Then open the conversation by describing your own move rather than your cofounder’s. If you have been taking the wheel, say so, name the specific behaviors that concern you about the business, and ask how you may be contributing to the problem.

If you have been underwater, tell your cofounder you are struggling. In my experience, that disclosure often brings a willingness to invest in your development, because a cofounder’s knowledge of the company is difficult to replace.

From there, change how decisions get made. Write down who owns which calls, and agree on what being consulted means as distinct from being informed. Decide before the next deadlock how a tie on a cofounder-level decision will be broken, whether by the CEO, by the larger shareholder, or by bringing in a cofounder coach or mediator, and put it in your cofounder agreement.

Expect to revisit the arrangement as the company grows and as your lives change. Part of that work is grieving the partner you imagined at the outset, so you can build a structure around the one you have, ideally while the two of you still like each other.

article continues after advertisement

item.title: Knowing When to Leave a Job
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Knowing When to Leave a Job

Signs your workplace won't change, and how to weigh the costs of staying.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Destructive leadership is linked to poorer well-being, lower performance, and stronger intentions to quit.
  • How a leader responds to concerns, and whether real change follows, signals whether staying makes sense.
  • Research links psychological safety to team learning behaviors like seeking feedback and discussing errors.
  • Weigh what a job gives you against what it costs your health, self-esteem, and relationships.

A former student* of mine came back to visit a few years after she had graduated. She works in finance, a heavily male-dominated industry, and even though she sees herself as a strong woman, she felt some traditional sexism seeping into the office culture. She was often asked to take notes or make coffee, something her male counterparts were rarely tasked with.

Chronic overwork and dismissive leadership takes a real toll.
Source: PixelWanderer/Pixabay

Even worse, the workplace culture was one in which the job was expected to be number one in employees’ lives, above everything else. Employees were often expected to stay late to work on unexpected, urgent problems, regardless of their availability. People routinely had to work weekends and late evenings, often without advance notice. When my former student raised these issues with her boss, she would be loudly berated and chastised. She described an environment with frequent turnover and no real sense of autonomy.

During our visit, she told me about a conversation with her boss in which she said it was a problem that employees had no psychological safety in the workplace. Her boss had never heard the term before and dismissed it outright. Hearing how he responded to her concerns, I couldn’t help but think, “Well, there’s your warning sign!”

In coaching her through the situation, I suspected she’d need to start looking for new employment opportunities. The toxic workplace she described seemed unlikely to change as long as her boss was in charge, as he didn’t seem interested in addressing any of the issues she raised.

What is psychological safety? The concept, extensively studied by Harvard professor Dr. Amy Edmondson, refers to the shared belief among team members that one can speak up in the workplace, offering countering perspectives or concerns, without the fear of retribution or punishment. Psychological safety gives team members room to ask questions, seek help, and learn when something doesn’t go as planned. In her foundational study of 51 workplace teams, Edmondson (1999) found that psychological safety was associated with team learning behaviors, such as seeking feedback, discussing errors, and asking for help. These are everyday interactions that allow people to learn and do their jobs effectively.

But what happens when your workplace lacks psychological safety? And when that’s compounded by a lack of work-life boundaries? How do you know when to stick it out with a company versus when it may be time to move on? A few questions can help you decide.

A few questions can help you determine whether now is the right time to leave your job.
Source: StockSnap/Pixabay

What happens when you raise a concern?

Does your supervisor listen and ask questions? Or do they respond with a knee-jerk reaction, resorting to ridicule, anger, or retaliation? No one is perfect. It can be challenging for leaders (even with the best of intentions) to hear critical feedback. But after they’ve had time to reflect, do they circle back to address the issue? Or does the situation end with dismissiveness, deflection, or retribution?

article continues after advertisement

Is there evidence that change is possible?

When a problem is raised, is there follow-through from leadership? Are there sustained changes in behavior (not just promises after someone threatens to quit)? In academia, the government, and other large organizations, change can be slow. You can’t always expect an immediate change in policy or procedure, especially if there’s a shared decision-making process involved. But have the wheels been put into motion? The speed of change matters, but so does whether there’s any meaningful movement at all.

What options exist within the organization?

Is there another supervisor or a transfer opportunity that could move you from the troubled department or unit into one that functions more smoothly? Could you switch teams or responsibilities so you work with different people or report to someone else? Can anyone serve as an ally in the situation, such as another supervisor or manager who can mediate?

What is staying costing you?

Research gives us reason to take the costs associated with a crummy job situation seriously. A meta-analysis by Schyns and Schilling (2013) found that destructive leadership was associated with poorer employee well-being, lower performance, and greater intentions to leave. The effects of a difficult working environment can extend beyond how you feel about your boss.

Consider your confidence, health (mental and physical), relationships, and ability to do work you feel good about. If you love the job and feel passionate about what you’re doing, you may be willing to put up with certain issues, like occasional late evenings or a sometimes snappy response from a supervisor. But if the job is wearing down your self-esteem and damaging your relationships outside of work because mandatory overtime means cancelled plans and missed social engagements, it may be time to consider the toll it’s taking on your life overall.

It’s almost never easy to leave a job, especially when you’ve landed your “dream job” and the job market is tight, making alternatives feel limited. Recognizing that it’s time to leave also doesn’t mean you're financially or practically able to leave right away. It may mean starting to explore your options and making a plan.

article continues after advertisement

I wouldn’t suggest jumping ship at the first sign of trouble. When it’s safe and reasonable to do so, give your supervisor and your workplace a chance to make things right. But if your concerns aren’t taken seriously and meaningful change seems unlikely, consider both what the job gives you (a paycheck, purpose, opportunities) and what it’s taking from you (work-life balance, self-esteem, health, relationships).

Sure, there are busy or difficult seasons of work. But if the scales are constantly tipped toward work at the expense of your health and life outside of it, it may be time to make a change.

*Some details have been changed to protect the students’ privacy. Story shared with permission.

item.title: The Impact of a Late Autism Diagnosis
item.description:
Autism

The Impact of a Late Autism Diagnosis

Making sense of your eating disorder recovery.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Upwards of 37% of individuals with a diagnosed eating disorder present with autistic traits.
  • Autistic identification builds new context into the function of eating disorders.
  • Without identification, a person’s lived experiences can be pathologized, rather than understood.
  • A diagnosis comes with complex emotions, but is beneficial for context and deepened understanding.

New research has shown that upwards of 37% of individuals with a diagnosed eating disorder present with autistic traits (Tchanturia et al., 2020). Understanding this overlap matters for treatment outcomes. The identification of autistic individuals with eating disorders builds new context into the function of the disorder and emphasizes the necessity of neuro-affirming treatment approaches.

Source: Hiki App/Unsplash

Due to our culture’s increased awareness of neurodivergence, we’ve seen more individuals seeking out autism diagnoses. Among those diagnosed, many are adults who weren’t identified as children. An autism diagnosis can have a big emotional impact. Suddenly, a person gets answers for how their brain works and why certain things are hard for them. These answers can act as crucial pieces of information in eating disorder recovery.

Both personally and professionally, I’ve watched the impact of having an autism diagnosis on a person’s eating disorder recovery. I was diagnosed as autistic at the age of 31, and I have a history of an eating disorder. Through my autism diagnosis, I started to better understand myself. This understanding helped me to edit the shame-based narratives I had been holding onto, like the belief that I was broken. I was also able to better accommodate my needs and build a more sustainable life for my recovery.

I’m not the only one with a story like this. I’ve worked with many folks whose diagnosis became an essential part of their recovery, helping them make sense of their experiences and providing a new framework for the support they need.

An autism diagnosis changes how you understand your history

When someone with an eating disorder receives an autism diagnosis later in life, they have new context for the history of their disorder. After my diagnosis, I remember looking back at my years of symptoms, treatment, and recovery attempts with a new perspective.

I was able to develop a deeper understanding of why the disorder developed, and why traditional treatment approaches weren’t successful in building long-term recovery. Now, as a therapist, I do go through a similar discovery process with my neurodivergent clients.

Source: Anthony Tran/Unsplash

In a paper published in 2025 by Downs and Adams, two clinicians write about their experiences of being late-diagnosed autistic and having eating disorders. In the paper, they discuss the critical role a lack of social support played in the development of their disorders.

They write, “For both of us, the absence of social support was not merely a backdrop of our experiences; it was a central force that shaped our illness trajectories. The lack of recognition for our neurodivergence created environments in which our struggles were misunderstood or overlooked, in turn compounding our sense of isolation (Downs & Adams, 2025).”

article continues after advertisement

This is just one example of an autism diagnosis changing how you understand your history.

In addition to the social impact autistic individuals face, a diagnosis can contextualize traits like sensory processing differences, literal thinking, rigidity, unique capacity for demands, and burnout. Eating disorder symptoms can overlap with autistic traits (Tchanturia et al., 2020). If autism isn’t identified, then a person’s lived experiences can end up being pathologized, rather than properly understood and supported.

When misunderstood, these traits may compound an illness’s progression over a person’s life. But with a diagnosis, a potentially compassionate context can be built, understanding can deepen, and neuro-affirming treatment approaches can be added.

Grieving the diagnosis and finding self-compassion

Getting diagnosed as autistic late in life can bring up a whole spectrum of emotions and questions. People report feeling a mix of relief, grief, anxiety, confusion, and compassion as they try to make sense of this new information. This makes sense.

I heard someone describe a late autism diagnosis like this: It’s like watching a movie that has a surprise ending, except the movie is your life. So now, when you go back and rewatch the movie of your life, you know the ending and therefore see everything in a new light.

Source: Land O'Lakes, Inc./Unsplash

Complicated questions can arise, such as:

  • Why didn’t anyone diagnose me sooner?
  • How could my life have been different if I had this information growing up?
  • Would my experiences with eating disorder treatment have been more successful if my treatment had used neuro-affirming approaches to care from the beginning?
  • What does that mean for my life and recovery moving forward?
article continues after advertisement

Questions and big emotions are part of the process. You’re allowed to feel whatever you’re feeling. Receiving a diagnosis is a big piece of information, and it can change how you see yourself and the world.

But even though a diagnosis accompanies a complex range of reactions, emotions, thoughts, and grief, people are beginning to explore the benefits of having answers. A 2024 study by French, Cassidy, & et al., called “Going Through Life on Hard Mode”—The Experience of Late Diagnosis of Autism and/or ADHD, interviewed seven health care professionals and 13 late-diagnosed adults. Through these interviews, it was discovered that a diagnosis was overall beneficial, as it offered a broader understanding and context for relationships and mental and physical well-being.

More research is needed to get a clearer picture from a larger sample, but it shows that getting a diagnosis can be beneficial, even if it comes late in life. However, nuance exists around identification and official diagnoses, and these aspects shouldn’t be overlooked.

Closing thoughts

Many complex factors can influence whether someone pursues a diagnostic process, and this same 2024 study by French, Cassidy, et al. showed the importance of considering timing and readiness before committing. Ethical, financial, and accessibility considerations also matter.

Getting an autism diagnosis late in life is a personal choice. But it can change how a person with an eating disorder understands their illness. A diagnosis can add important context to someone’s history and show why neuro-affirming treatment approaches are necessary.

item.title: Psychiatry: In the Crosshairs, at a Crossroads
item.description:
Psychiatry

Psychiatry: In the Crosshairs, at a Crossroads

An open letter to save our field.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • The field of psychiatry is currently under threat, and we are not responding effectively.
  • Psychiatrists need to move towards, not away from, the things that make us unique.
  • Specific steps we can take include returning to more in-person care, and moving away from "med checks."

This is not an anti-psychiatry post. I love my profession. I have seen it literally save lives and pull people out of very deep holes. But the very existence of psychiatry is under threat, and we are not responding in an effective way.

My beloved colleagues, it is time for some tough love.

We currently have psychologists doing this work with no medical training. We have nurses doing this work with no psychotherapy training. And, of course, we have emerging AI technology and all of its corporate backers, looking for an opportunity to take this work away from human beings altogether.

Our essential problem is that we are playing right into their hands. At the precise time that we should be leaning into what distinguishes us from other mental health professionals (and chatbots), our practices are becoming more homogenized, restrictive, and impersonal. At the exact time that we need data to support the defense of our field, we are spending our research time and money elsewhere. Meanwhile, our well-meaning but somewhat distracted professional organizations are so focused on fending off ridiculous attacks from external forces, including some from our own government, that we are failing to challenge and affect change with the group where we have the most leverage: ourselves.

Here is what we need to do if we want to save our field.

  1. Come back to in-person care. Yes, telemedicine has an important role in mental health care, but we’ve vastly overplayed this hand. We like to tell people that telemedicine is all about patients, but the reality is that too often it is about us and our convenience and lifestyle. In balance, there is just too much clinically that is lost for too many people when care is given exclusively online. Continue this path, and we are practically begging to be replaced by AI.
  2. End the 15-minute med check. Psychiatry was founded on some core principles. Among those is that human beings are complex, and that our relationship with patients and caregivers is an essential component of people getting better. We’ve lost that, too often moving to a quick “symptom and side effect” model of care that may pay the bills but makes psychiatry less effective, less human, and, frankly, less fun.
  3. Take insurance. While mental health problems can affect anyone, they are disproportionately found among those with lower financial resources. At the same time, psychiatrists are the most likely medical specialists to refuse to take medical insurance, particularly Medicaid. These two things mean that psychiatrists are not meeting the clinical needs of many communities, with that gap being filled by other types of clinicians. If we wish to remain relevant, if we wish to be supported and valued by the communities we serve, we have to be there for everyone, not just rich people.
  4. Put us to the test. It is well past time for some rigorous and comprehensive studies on psychiatric care quality that examine practical, real-world outcomes. Are patients really getting better? Are we following best practice guidelines? What factors support better patient outcomes? I continue to hold the belief that, on average, a well-trained, well-performing psychiatrist can deliver the best care for patients. It’s high time we prove that. The longer we wait, the more folks will be able to make vague equivalency claims to justify cutting us out of the picture.
article continues after advertisement

I’m approaching retirement and not particularly concerned about my own personal job security. The worry is for my younger colleagues and for the future of my profession. Already we are being challenged to justify our increased salary, our more intensive training, our loftier status, and there just isn’t much data we can point to right now in our defense. How do we rationalize the need for medical training when we don’t even get vital signs at our online appointments? How do we defend the need for psychotherapy training when we don’t even use it in our 15-minute med checks? How can we tell an insurance company that the more expensive care we deliver is best when we don’t study it?

It is not too late. There is still a lot of excellent work being done, often in close collaboration with other types of medical and mental health professionals. There are “movements” afoot to improve our approach and the quality of care we provide in order to revitalize our field. This is where we need to focus, right now, if we are to remain healthy as a field in a world full of economic and technological change.

item.title: Are You the Family Scapegoat?
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Are You the Family Scapegoat?

When one family member is named the villain, the rest get to ignore the pattern.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Every family is governed by unwritten rules; the scapegoat is often the one who dares to break them.
  • When one person is crowned as the family problem, everyone else gets to avoid examining their part.
  • After years of being cast as the villain, you might start believing the family's version of your truth.
  • Perhaps healing begins when you stop arguing for acceptance that asks you to betray yourself.
Source: Getty Images / Unsplash

There’s something exceedingly painful about feeling as though you're standing on the outside, alone in the cold with your nose pressed against the glass, looking in on your family.

You want to be looked at and introduced the same way your siblings are. You wish Mom or Dad would say your name with the same fondness they say theirs. You feel like you're not in the club, but hope to be granted access.

All the while, no one admits to you being the outsider.

The thing is, families rarely hold meetings to announce, “You’ve been selected as our designated problem!” Scapegoating is far subtler than that.

Every Family Has Rules: Most Aren’t Written Down

As a therapist, my job is to keep in mind the other characters in my client’s life, even if none are in my room.

Families are governed by rules that are seldom spoken but powerfully felt. Perhaps everyone knows to tiptoe through the hallway when Dad cracks open a six-pack, or to speak about the lawsuit in hushed whispers, or to never mention the uncle who hasn't appeared at Grandma's doorstep in decades.

And while family members are organized into roles that maintain a homeostasis, from the golden child to the black sheep, no person can be reduced to any label they’ve been assigned, no matter how stubbornly its members wish to uphold it.

Every family system under the sun fights to stay the same. And if you challenge that predictable climate? You might be met with red-hot fury or panic.

Maybe not overtly, and certainly not admittedly, but you may be cast as the villain: criticized, undermined, or iced out of the coalition.

Sometimes the "least-liked family member,” the scapegoat, is the person onto whom unwanted tension or shame is most conveniently projected, because if the problem lives inside him or her, nobody else has to examine what lives between "us."

The scapegoat isn't necessarily behaving beautifully. Sometimes their pain does manifest as unsavory. Sometimes they are the one causing a scene. In some cases, the scapegoated family member is hallmarked by addiction, depression, or stormy relationships.

The point isn't that every accusation against them is false, but that one person's behavior can become an opportune explanation for an entire family's unchecked malaise. Because once a family decides where the smoke is coming from, they can conveniently stop asking what’s striking the match.

My client, Allison*, never dreamed of coming to therapy. But, after a massive family blowup left her feeling as though she’d been shoved onto the lonely pavement, she found her way to my door.

I soon learned that heavy conversations weren't allowed in her home. Everyone was to obey an unspoken rule: Mask your sorrow until you can unpack it alone, if at all.

But Allison was a precocious, sensitive soul who struggled with not naming what she saw. She was both fascinated and tormented by the untravelled grooves of the unsaid.

"I'm wired a little differently than my siblings," she lamented during a session.

Once, at age 9, Allison watched cautiously as her mom wiped tears from bloodshot eyes while setting the Thanksgiving table. Her dad stomped through the candlelit dining room, hissing expletives and shooting daggers in his wife's direction, all while her sisters obediently munched popcorn with eyes glued to screens.

Later, when Allison curiously tapped her mom on the shoulder, she was swatted away and accused of being "too sensitive."

Allison had challenged the rules that fastened the dynamic together. And she would find herself in similar conundrums for decades. When she challenged the rules, she was tossed to the wrong side of an energetic brick wall. But when she followed them, she was ushered inside, only to then feel like a traitor to her own heart.

Sometimes the "Problem Child" Is Carrying a Family-Sized Problem

Once somebody is assigned the identity of “troubled” or “different,” new information is then filtered through the old story.

Their anger proves they're angry. Their reactions prove they're dramatic. Their rebuttals prove they're combative. Eventually, even their self-protection becomes evidence: "I told you she doesn't care."

As adults, scapegoated family members may become the ones who visit the least. Perhaps it's because they're struggling with the consequences of poor choices. Or, perhaps, it's because they can no longer play by rules that hurt them; they're unwilling to swallow the truth, yet lack the safety to air it. In the presence of this unsafety, they cope by escaping.

In religious families, the scapegoat is often the one being prayed for the most. And, sadly, in my clinical observations, family members aren't necessarily praying to better understand or support them. Oftentimes they're praying for compliance — for them to stop challenging the status quo, or to return to a version of themselves that makes everyone more comfortable.

When the Family Story Becomes Your Story About Yourself

What happens after years of being treated as the one everyone “blames” or “worries about”? Eventually, the family doesn't have to be in the room, because the scapegoat is holding the courtroom within.

If this resonates, you might explore asking yourself these questions:

  • Do you chronically over-explain?
  • Do you panic when someone’s upset with you?
  • Do you gather evidence that you're “worthy” or “good”?
  • Do you fixate on who's being praised or prioritized?
  • Do you dream of winning over the family member least willing to see you differently?

Who Are You, Really? You Get to Decide

When you’re small, you have no say in the messages your attachment figures install into your self-identity.

But the beautiful news is that, now, you get to construct your own sense of personal worthiness and security. You cannot change the blueprint you inherited, but you get to rehabilitate and restore what your family dynamics may have stormed over and damaged.

From here on out, you're the architect of your self-concept. You get to determine who you are... and who you aren’t.

As for Allison, her breakthrough wasn't about anyone in her family changing, but about accepting that she'd spent years presenting evidence to a jury committed to a verdict she couldn’t support. It was about exploring more empowering, wise, and self-supportive ways of participating in the familial cycle—without being swallowed whole by the ache to be accepted.

In this spirit, let's say you've spent your life standing in the cold, nose pressed against the glass. If so, perhaps your healing is about realizing that you’re not required to spend the rest of your days aimlessly waiting there. Especially if it means being a traitor to your own heart.

*Name and identifying details changed to protect client confidentiality.

item.title: The Shadow Side of Nervous System Regulation
item.description:
Neuroscience

The Shadow Side of Nervous System Regulation

Regulation is not the goal of life.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Shadow is not evil; it is what we refuse to look at in ourselves, including our unlived lives.
  • Nervous-system language can help us understand ourselves, or help our ego avoid being meaningfully changed.
  • The body is not only something to calm; it is often psyche asking to be heard.
Source: Photo by wen panda on Unsplash

The nervous system is having a moment online. Scroll long enough on your chosen platform and you will find exercises and workbooks promising to regulate your nervous system sitting beside posts about vagal tone. As a psychotherapist who works daily with the unconscious and the body, I am glad people are getting curious about what lies underneath. Yet I am also uneasy, as much of nervous-system wellness culture seems to serve the very aspect of us that authentic inner work is meant to humble: the ego.

You have likely heard the language;

“That’s just my trauma response, and you’re dysregulating me.”
“My body is keeping the score, and that person is a trigger for me.”

Comments like these are something Jung would have recognized immediately: shadow wearing the costume of self-care.

So, let me be clear: this is not a total takedown of somatic psychology. I love the body; for years, I deliberately sought out somatic clinical supervision because the body is where so much of the work comes alive.

Nervous-system language has given many people their first words for experiences that once felt shameful or unnamed, and that matters. The point is not to call anyone out, but to call all of us in, and to get curious about what our wellness habits might be protecting us from.

What shadow is, and what it isn't

For Jung, shadow was never simply a synonym for evil. This psychological construct names the aspects of personality we refuse to deal with; the qualities that contradict our predominant (egoic) self-image, and the unlived lives that remain always present in us.1 This is also why shadow is so hard to work with, as it challenges who we believe we are, and it exists within the deepest places in the unconscious.

We all have ways of keeping shadow and other unconscious contents at a distance; psychodynamic therapists call these defenses.2 Most operate outside our awareness and protect us from knowing what feels too painful to know. We may consistently blame others or push difficult feelings out of mind through repression. Other times, we can project what we cannot own onto the people around us, and sometimes onto the most thoughtful people in our lives. In doing so, we protect ourselves at the cost of accountability.

Over two thousand years ago, the Roman playwright Terence wrote, “I am human; nothing human is alien to me”.3 I encountered this line through Dr. James Hollis, who calls it perhaps the wisest thing ever said about the shadow.4 Hollis invites us to recognize that we carry the same capacities as the people we judge, whether literally or symbolically. He discusses how the murderer in us, for instance, may never harm another person; instead, it may be quietly murdering our own creative life.

article continues after advertisement

When shadow goes unexamined, people can become possessed by it. One of its most common forms is being caught up in our own sense of rightness. Jung himself believed that tending to our own shadow is a gift not only to ourselves but to the whole world.5 So, the shadow shows up in tangible ways in our relationships and communities, and attempting to integrate one’s shadow is a real form of social responsibility.

The shadow of nervous-system culture

Every framework creates stories, and a story that is never reflected upon will eventually run the person who tells it. Wellness language can serve the same protective function as any other defenses. "I’m just dysregulated" can be an honest observation, but it can also work as a kind of intellectualization; naming a state in borrowed clinical terms so that we never have to feel, or wonder about, what set it off.

"Protecting my peace" can be a genuine healthy boundary, or it can be avoidance dressed up as self-care, a way of steering around a hard conversation that is ours to have. The Jungian question is not only how do I calm this… but what in me is trying to stay unconscious? What is psyche actually asking of me here?

It is worth asking, honestly:

  • Whose needs does my wellness practice serve: my authentic growth, or my need to feel in control?
  • If I let go of this framework, who would I be, and which community would stop recognizing me?
  • When I reach for regulation, what feeling am I refusing to let finish its sentence?
  • Am I answerable to my soul, or only to my nervous system?
  • What in me needs this nervous-system approach to be the right framework?
article continues after advertisement

These questions point toward something the ego would rather not see: its own quiet self-absorption, which lives in all of us. That is what makes them shadow questions.

When the ego wants to run the nervous system

The ego is useful, and I love that it helps us tie our shoes or tend to daily responsibilities. Yet, the ego is also a conservative agent, often intimidated by change. Listen to how it speaks: I wish to manage this, or I wish to control this.

As you can likely now see, nervous-system language hands the ego a sophisticated new vocabulary. Even breathwork, mindfulness, or other transcendental practices can be recruited as one more thing to master, so that the practice meant to soften control becomes its most refined instrument.

Regulation is not the goal of life

Regulation is not the goal of life, and neither is happiness, which is transient and contextual. A body that is ALWAYS being calmed is a body that is rarely allowed to speak. Sometimes the tremor, collapse, or a sensation of heat in the chest is not a state to be shifted, but psyche asking to be inner-stood.

At the end of the day, we are built to change, grow old, and die. The more sovereign and controlling we try to be over our nervous systems, the more we will likely suffer neurotically.

Shadow work, in the body or anywhere else, does not ask us to become calmer all the time. Instead, shadow asks us to become more whole; to meet what we have refused, take back what we have projected, and live a life of meaning that can hold suffering honestly rather than flee it.

You are not separate from nature; you are nature, and nature asks to be lived.

item.title: How Politics and Mental Health Intersect
item.description:
Politics

How Politics and Mental Health Intersect

A Personal Perspective: Current priorities may increase psychological distress.

Posted October 23, 2026

Key points
  • Other rich nations invest much more in the needs of children and families.
  • Americans may not recognize that help is missing because we never had it in the first place.
  • Our mental health as a nation could improve if federal policies prioritized taking care of one another.
Source: Nadezhada Buraveleva/istock

In my office: “I didn’t expect it to be so hard,” says the mother who just gave birth, the parent who is raising young children, or the young adult trying to live independently after college. There are many psychological reasons these transitional times are difficult; I listen carefully to understand the stressors my patients are facing, and then use all the clinical tools at my disposal to provide support.

That said, I also recognize their worries are amplified because of a federal government that hasn’t always cared to invest in their well-being. It may be a more difficult transition due to a lack of infrastructure support.

No Infrastructure Support After Birth

Let’s start with birth. A family is sent home a few days after delivery, with some information and a 6-week OB-GYN follow-up. The addition of a baby adds financial and emotional stress; if you are lucky, you live in one of the 14 states, or Washington, DC, that provide mandatory paid family leave, or one of the nine that support voluntary leave, paid through private insurance. So many are left without support: There is no federal program protecting wages after childbirth.

Nurturing an infant is a high-intensity, 24/7 job. Family and friends may pitch in. If you have resources, you can pay for help and child care. Families at the poverty level are eligible for Early Head Start or Medicaid, which can provide additional family and infant assistance, but the services don’t erase the stress of a new baby on a limited income. Most people reside in the middle, making too much to qualify for Early Head Start but not enough to access the care they need

A small smattering of states (MA, NJ, OR) and local areas offer some postpartum clinical care, but universal federal support is lacking.

The outpouring of female support for Lindsay Clancy, the mother who murdered her children while in the throes of postpartum psychosis, reflects how many women understand the feeling of being insufficiently supported during the postpartum period. What is currently offered is wholly inadequate.

In contrast, in the UK, all new parents receive a midwife visit within 36 hours of birth. Necessary follow-up is provided until care is handed off to a clinician about two weeks after birth for continued support to the infant and the mother.

No Infrastructure Support Before Kindergarten

There is extensive research documenting how early childhood education (ECE) is associated with improved cognitive, psychological, and medical outcomes years later. ECE teachers are experts in child development and a resource for parents. ECE supports parental employment, and provides protected time so parents can address their own medical needs.

article continues after advertisement

For the majority of families, preschool is a huge expense. Like postpartum care, there are some state- or city-funded preschool programs, but these are outliers.

A general pattern emerges. If you have a lot of resources, you can pay for what you need. Low-income families will struggle with day-to-day expenses, but the child will be eligible for Headstart, a funded federal preschool option that the current administration is trying to deregulate. The group in the middle is left to fend for themselves. There is no federal program supporting all young families.

In contrast, several European countries provide heavily subsidized or free preschool. In a 2021 UNICEF report assessing rich nations' investment in childcare, the U.S. ranked second to last.

Americans don’t even notice the assistance is missing because we never had it in the first place.

No Infrastructure for College, Housing, and Healthcare.

On to education, housing, and healthcare: The costs of all three have exploded over the last several years without governmental programs to address the gap between costs and wages. The enhanced federal tax credits for the Affordable Care Act have expired. There are some federal safety nets, Medicare and Social Security being most well-known. While these programs are critically important, they leave most Americans without assistance during much of their life.

The American Ideal Is Hurtful

Somehow, this approach has become a story of American resilience. We are a tough people, and if you can’t make it, if you can’t afford childcare, or health care or housing, well, that’s on you. Wanting help somehow makes you a taker, a dead weight, or a potential parasite on the system.

This theory works well for politicians funded by billionaires and corporations. The “trickle down” economic theory, that taking care of businesses and the wealthy will allow wealth to trickle down to those less fortunate, has been promoted ad nauseam my entire adult life — and evidence shows it doesn’t work.

article continues after advertisement

The system has been weighted against the average American for years. Why is it especially impacting mental health now? Decades ago, rent was cheaper and a mortgage was attainable. Wages could keep up with living expenses. The Affordable Care Act provided a safety net before it was systematically diminished. It was easier to dream.

Now, it feels harder because it is. What is it like to enter your 20s and be unable to find a job that will cover rent? What desperation causes a person to start a GoFundMe for necessary medical care?

It’s no surprise that anxiety and depression are up.

What If We Prioritized Taking Care of One Another?

I hope, before I retire, that I see an American economy and federal government that redefines patriotism as unabashedly, unashamedly, investing in all people at all ages. Imagine a government that would prioritize policies for student and family aid, that would protect and subsidize health care, and ease the cost of housing. Care for all stages of the life cycle would be considered. Just because we haven’t seen it happen, doesn’t mean that it couldn’t. I believe our individual psychological health would improve if our values and votes focused on meeting the needs of all Americans, from sea to shining sea.
